summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland runs on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 a person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker, their first name, or both by personal declaration before a civil registrar. The route requires no surgery, no medical diagnosis and no court proceeding. About 350 people had used it in its first months, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022.

Marriage for All has been in force since 1 July 2022, opening civil marriage to same-sex couples together with adoption and access to IVF; the reform passed a referendum with 64.1% approval. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised on the same terms as any other couple.

Federal criminal law protects against discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. Since 1 July 2020, public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on those grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis of the Criminal Code. Switzerland has no general hate-crime provision; ODIHR's 2024 country report notes that hate crimes are handled through the anti-discrimination provisions and that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, with police not recording bias motivation. The available sources do not record an equivalent federal criminal provision enumerating gender identity. UNHCR's country guidance records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime runs at roughly six cases a week. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline recorded 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons, covering 2026 to 2030. It rests on three pillars: support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence. The Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinates implementation.

Employment protection covers name and gender presentation at work. Employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Art. 328ff of the Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act. Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.

In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name. The court held that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.

Conversion therapy is unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions; the measure remains pending in the Council of States. Neuchâtel banned the practice in 2023, and Valais and Vaud in 2024. The Federal Council has stated that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to the young people subjected to them, and that they breach professional duties; a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open.

Detention placement for trans people has no federal provision and is handled cantonally, with no Swiss case law on the subject and no special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice. Basel-Stadt's detention law, adopted by its Grand Council on 13 November 2019, requires the separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible; the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Support infrastructure includes a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) with helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland, which advises on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum.
tangentialFactors:
Blood donation rules changed on 1 November 2023 to a four-month deferral after the last new sexual contact for gay men, down from one year since 2017.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page for Switzerland reports an overall index score and per-category compliance ratings, assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes; the available sources do not reproduce the scores themselves.
localsOnly:
A 2018 survey of 1,700 schoolchildren aged 14 and 15 in Neuchâtel found that 10% of girls and 5% of boys identified as LGBT. Among respondents, 38% reported receiving slaps, kicks or punches, 25% reported frequent harassment, 16% reported being a victim of physical violence, and 7% reported discrimination by a teacher.

An annual Coming Out Day has been observed in schools, high schools and universities since the mid-1990s, often through seminars, films and group discussions. LGBT youth groups operate at EPFL, ETH Zurich, Lausanne and St. Gallen.
outOfScopeNotes: The age at which a minor may change legal sex without guardian consent is unresolved. Minors aged 12 to 18 originally required guardian consent; the National Council suppressed that requirement while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which consent is needed. The wording finally in force is not established by the available sources.
